City of Cincinnati*, 114 N.E.3d 805, at 820 (Ohio Com. Pl. 2018)(police services are “core or basic governmental services of a large municipality”), citing *Foley v. Connelie*, 435 U.S. 291, 297 (1978)(“[a] discussion of the police function is essentially a description of one of the basic functions of government... The police function fulfills a most fundamental obligation of government to its constituency”); *Heck v. City of Freeport*, 985 F.2d 305, 309 (7th Cir. 1993)(identifying the “basic services” of government as “police and fire protection . . .”); *Drees Co. v. Hamilton Twp.*, 2012-Ohio-2370, at ¶ 22-23, 31-32 (“…the fact that the revenue is earmarked for police protection, fire protection, road improvement, and parks that benefit the entire community is the key factor. The assessments raise revenue for the public's benefit. All members of the community will benefit from improved roadways and parks, as well as from consistent levels of police and fire protection”)(emphasis added).

Here, the Alarm Assessments, which the City claims funds policing, are not calibrated to account for (1) the amounts Plaintiffs and others have already contributed to the cost of policing in their roles as taxpayers; or (2) the City’s preexisting obligation to provide police protection irrespective of payment.

In conclusion, even holding all else aside, the City’s Alarm Assessments impose an unconstitutional condition on Plaintiffs’ exercise of their rights to speak and petition and to defend self, family, and property

# IV. Conclusion

The logic underlying the City’s attempt to convert policing from a core governmental function to a privatized proprietary function is without a limiting principle in scope or amount. This cannot be, and fortunately is not, the law. Consequently, this Court must reverse the Trial Court’s erroneous Entry denying Plaintiffs’ Motion for Summary Judgment, which sought to declare the City of Cincinnati’s prohibition on security alarm usage without prior payment of an arbitrary assessment unconstitutional, and to enjoin the same, and granting Defendants’ Motion for Summary Judgment on the same topic.

[^4]: See inter alia, McIntyre v. Ohio Elections Comm'n, No. 90AP-1221, 1992 WL 230505, at 6 (Ohio Ct. App. Apr. 7, 1992), aff'd sub nom. McIntyre v. Ohio Elections Comm., 1993-Ohio-224, 67 Ohio St. 3d 391 (“Unlike the First Amendment to the United States Constitution, the Ohio constitutional provision expressly gives to each citizen not only the right to speak but, also, the right both to write and to publish sentiments on any subject . . . The Ohio Supreme Court has recognized the broad scope of the Ohio constitutional protection for the freedom of expression of sentiments”).
[^5]: At this point, an important proviso may assist this Court: a regulation need not be a total prohibition of speech to impermissibly infringe upon protected expression. “The power to impose a license tax on the exercise of [first amendment] freedoms is indeed as potent as the power of censorship which this Court has repeatedly struck down.” Century Fed., Inc. v. City of Palo Alto, 710 F. Supp. 1559, 1561–62 (N.D. Cal. 1988), citing, inter alia, Murdock v. Pennsylvania, 319 U.S. 105, 111, and 113 (1943) (citations omitted); Cox v. New Hampshire, 312 U.S. 569, 576–78 (1941). In the seminal case of Murdock, the Supreme Court declared that “[f]reedom of speech ... [must be] available to all, not merely to those who can pay their own way,” that “[a] state may not impose a charge for the enjoyment of a right granted by the federal constitution,” and that “the power to tax the exercise of a [constitutional] privilege is the power to control or suppress its enjoyment.” “Thus, any effort by a government to impose a tax upon the means or instruments used to engage exclusively in First Amendment rights, as well as doing so by targeting a small segment of the population, presents a very real potential to destroy, i.e., to stifle, the meaningful and effective exercise of such rights.” Lamar Advantage, infra., at 816-818. Thus, it is not significant to this Court’s analysis that the Alarm Ban “merely” imposes a monetary charge as a prerequisite to otherwise-protected communication rather than imposing a death sentence in response to communication.
